chapters.title: Chapter 4: Country Risk and Your Portfolio

lessons.title: Building a Country Risk Checklist for International Investing

children.text: Sixteen lessons ago, this course started with a simple question: why do governments borrow at all? Everything since has built toward a single, practical goal, giving you a working checklist you can actually run through before putting money into any market outside your own. This final lesson pulls every framework built across four chapters into that one usable tool.

body.title: Country Risk Checklist for International Investing
steps: Check the twin deficits: is the fiscal deficit and the current account deficit trend widening or narrowing?
Check debt composition: what share of government debt is domestic versus foreign-currency, and how concentrated is the maturity profile (any 'debt wall')?
Check reserve adequacy: is import cover above roughly 3 months, and do reserves cover short-term external debt (the Greenspan-Guidotti rule)?
Check the sovereign rating from all three major agencies, not just one, and note the outlook direction, not only the letter grade
Check the market's own pricing: bond spreads or CDS, and whether they are moving in line with, or diverging from, the official rating
Check the political risk pillar: governance and institutional quality, upcoming elections, and policy continuity risk
Identify whether recent capital inflows into the country are structural, cyclical, or event-driven, since each reverses under different conditions
Check what kind of foreign capital dominates: sticky FDI and long-term capital, or flightier FPI equity and short-duration debt
If considering local-currency debt or equity, price in the currency risk explicitly rather than being drawn in by a high headline yield alone
Check your own currency exposure and confirm you are not making an unpriced, unexamined currency bet in either direction
Check your own country's capital account rules and regulatory constraints on moving money in or out, since these can change

body.caption: Where Each Checklist Item Comes From

cells: Twin deficits, debt composition, reserve adequacy
Credit ratings, outlook, and market pricing (spreads and CDS)
Capital flow type, stickiness, and currency risk pricing
Your own currency bet and home-country regulatory constraints

children.text: Running the Checklist: A Worked Example
Consider a hypothetical country, referred to here simply as Country Z, being evaluated for a potential bond allocation.

cells: Reserves cover only about 70% of short-term external debt
BB+ (one notch below investment grade), negative outlook from two of three agencies
Widened from 350 to 700 basis points over the last six months
A general election is due in four months; the incumbent government has signalled likely pre-election fiscal loosening
Dominated by short-duration FPI debt; minimal FDI

body.title: Run the Checklist on Country Z
body.scenario: Use the Country Z snapshot above alongside the checklist from this lesson.
body.prompt: Identify the two or three most serious red flags in this profile, and explain what stage of the four-stage crisis anatomy from Chapter 3 this country appears to be approaching, if the current trajectory continues.
body.modelAnswer: Three red flags stand out. First, the Greenspan-Guidotti rule is failing: reserves cover only about 70% of short-term external debt, a genuine warning sign even though import cover at 4.2 months looks superficially comfortable. Second, the CDS spread has doubled in six months while the rating has only moved to negative outlook, a classic sign, from Chapter 2, that the market is repricing risk faster than the rating agencies, often a leading indicator of a future downgrade. Third, the combination of an election in four months with signalled pre-election fiscal loosening threatens to widen the already elevated twin deficits further, adding a domestic political trigger on top of already-thin reserve buffers. Taken together, with a foreign-currency-heavy debt load, thin reserve coverage of short-term debt, market pricing sharply worse than the rating, and a political trigger on the horizon, Country Z looks to be moving from Stage 1 (building vulnerability) into Stage 3 (loss of confidence), with a real risk of tipping into Stage 4 if the pre-election fiscal loosening actually materialises or if global risk sentiment sours further. A cautious investor would treat this as a country to avoid or significantly underweight until these signals stabilise or reverse.

body.title: Final Check
body.question: In Country Z's profile, why is the gap between its CDS spread movement and its official rating action particularly important to notice?
options: It is not important; ratings and CDS always move in lockstep

It suggests the market is pricing in deteriorating risk faster than the rating agencies have formally recognised, a pattern this course has flagged as a leading indicator of further downgrades or even a crisis
It means the CDS market has made a pricing error that will soon correct itself
It indicates the country's fiscal deficit has already improved
body.explanation: This is exactly the pattern covered in Chapter 2 and seen again in Sri Lanka's own build-up to default in Chapter 3: continuously traded market instruments like CDS and bond spreads often move well ahead of periodic, committee-driven rating actions. A sharp CDS widening alongside only a modest, lagging rating change is a signal worth taking seriously in its own right, not a reason to dismiss the market's pricing.

body.text: Country risk analysis is not one metric, one rating, or one headline. It is a checklist, run consistently, across every pillar this course has covered, because vulnerabilities compound quietly for years and then reveal themselves all at once. The work is in catching the quiet years.

children.text: That closes this course. You now have the same core framework analysts, rating agencies, and institutional investors use to size up a country before committing capital to it: why sovereigns borrow and who lends to them, how country risk breaks into economic, political, and currency pillars, how that risk gets priced through ratings, spreads, and CDS, what happens when it turns into an actual crisis, and how to apply all of it, in both directions, to your own investing decisions. Keep this checklist close. The specific numbers in any country's story will change constantly. The framework for reading them will not.

points: A complete country risk checklist covers debt composition and reserve adequacy, sovereign ratings and market pricing, political risk and crisis warning signs, and the type and stickiness of capital flows involved.
Always check whether market pricing (spreads, CDS) agrees with the official rating; a widening gap is itself a signal worth acting on.
When evaluating local-currency exposure, price the currency risk explicitly rather than being drawn in by yield alone.
The checklist applies in both directions: to foreign capital evaluating your own market, and to your own decisions when investing beyond it.
Country risk rarely arrives without warning. It arrives without enough people running the checklist during the quiet years when the warning signs were still just data points.

body.text: Country Z is a hypothetical, illustrative composite built to demonstrate how to apply this lesson's checklist, not a real country. All specific figures, ratings, and thresholds referenced across this course are approximate, illustrative, or time-bound, and should be verified against current official and market sources before being used in any real investment decision. This course is educational in nature and does not constitute investment advice.
